Department of Public Administration

Hyejin Kang 강혜진

Hello — I am Hyejin Kang.

Who enters public service, and how far they rise. I study how personnel systems, organizations, and political appointments to executive positions shape the way government works and what it achieves.

I am an Associate Professor and Graduate Program Chair in the Department of Public Administration at Dong-A University. I studied political science at Seoul National University and received my MA (2011) and PhD (2017) from its Graduate School of Public Administration, with a dissertation on ministerial influence and strategy in the departmental budget process.

My work centers on public personnel administration and organizational management and on political appointments, including presidential appointments of ministers — the subject of my National Research Foundation of Korea early-career project — alongside continuing research on trust in government and local public services. I combine panel analysis, quantile regression, and survival analysis with qualitative coding, grounded theory, and case study work.

Research

01

Public Personnel Administration

Balanced personnel policy, job autonomy and satisfaction by recruitment type, officials' self-assessed expertise, public service motivation and turnover intention, and the role perceptions and socialization of senior civil servants.

02

Political Appointments

Typologies of presidential appointments beyond the loyalty–competence dichotomy, balanced personnel among political appointees, ministerial influence and strategy in the budget process, and how appointment routes shape the behavior and performance of agency and local public enterprise heads.

03

Organizations & Leadership

Transformational and transactional leadership and unethical pro-organizational behavior, organizational commitment and goal ambiguity, organizational slack and multidimensional performance, external network management, and followership.

04

Trust & Local Government

Expectation–disconfirmation and local satisfaction, mechanisms of trust and distrust, e-government use, social capital and tolerance, and attitudes toward immigrant inclusion.
